title: Fundstrat's Tom Lee Points To 10x Forward PE As Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) Offers "Best Risk/Reward In AI" After Huang Exit - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 14, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A forward price-to-earnings multiple of 10 is the foundation of Tom Lee’s case for buying Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares following the departure of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. Lee, who heads research at Fundstrat, made the call on social media platform X as the chipmaker’s stock closed Thursday down roughly 4% at approximately $166.10, having recovered from an intraday collapse of as much as 14%. The stock has now shed 11% since the start of the year, leaving investors weighing whether the selloff represents a durable entry point or the beginning of a more prolonged correction. “There will be pain near term since many investors view this as an adverse development. It is. But at 10x forward PE, this is also the best risk/reward in AI at the moment,” Lee wrote. Lee acknowledged that any founder’s exit is a defining moment for a company, writing that “the departure of the founder and CEO is a massive test for any company.” Despite that concession, he argued that Nvidia’s structural advantages, including its chip-design lead, control over its supply chain, and the entrenched CUDA software ecosystem, would outlast the leadership transition. He also pointed to the depth of Nvidia’s engineering organization and its capacity to deploy free cash flow toward share buybacks as reasons the company could sustain its competitive position. Lee added that employee ownership aligns internal incentives with shareholders, claiming without citing a source that 80% of Nvidia staff qualify as stock millionaires and that half hold equity worth more than $25 million. The bullish Nvidia call arrived against a turbulent macro backdrop, with Bitcoin plunging roughly 7% in 24 hours to $68,408 by early Friday morning, its weakest level since August 20, while Ether fell 6% to $1,921. The crypto slide wiped out $1.47 billion in leveraged positions, with $1.31 billion of that representing forced exits from bullish bets, compounding pressure across risk assets broadly. Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds recorded $1.44 billion in net outflows across five sessions between November 5 and November 11, with BlackRock’s IBIT responsible for approximately $1.07 billion of that total, according to data from Farside Investors. A surging dollar added further strain, with the Dollar Index reaching a 19-month high after October consumer prices rose 0.4% on a monthly basis and core inflation climbed 0.3%, keeping additional Federal Reserve rate action in view. Index provider MSCI separately flagged Strategy and Metaplanet for removal from its benchmarks after the November 30 close, a move that could prompt mechanical selling by funds tracking those indexes. Lee, who chairs Bitmine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), has maintained a parallel conviction in Ethereum even as prices falter, saying that weakness in the token reflects “the impatience of markets” rather than any deterioration in fundamentals. Bitmine disclosed it purchased 9,587 ETH during the prior week, lifting its total holdings to 6.07 million tokens as of November 8, a position representing 4.97% of Ethereum’s entire circulating supply and just below the firm’s stated 5% target. Lee framed his longer-term crypto outlook around a 24-to-36-month horizon, citing accelerating tokenization activity concentrated on the Ethereum network as the primary catalyst. On Stocktwits, retail traders appeared to side with Lee on Nvidia, pushing sentiment to “extremely bullish” on “extremely high” message volume, while Bitcoin drew only a “neutral” reading on comparatively thin traffic. Bitcoin has declined 19% year-to-date, a steeper loss than Nvidia’s 11% pullback, underscoring the breadth of the current retreat from high-risk growth assets across both equity and digital markets. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Palantir's (NASDAQ: PLTR) P/E Of 219 And Nvidia's (NASDAQ: NVDA) Supply Crunch Define A High-Stakes Race To 2030 - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 14, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A valuation gap separating two of the AI era’s most prominent stocks may matter more to long-term investors than either company’s headline revenue growth. Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR), trading intraday at $161.94, carries a price-to-earnings ratio of 219 and a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 170, metrics that place extraordinary demands on future execution. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), changing hands at $188.84, faces a different constraint: its fiscal 2028 growth is expected to reach roughly 70%, a figure management says is bounded entirely by manufacturing supply rather than customer appetite. CEO Jensen Huang made the company’s position clear, telling analysts “Even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%.” Both stocks pulled back sharply in recent sessions, with Nvidia declining 11.62% and Palantir falling 17.55% over a single week, prompting fresh scrutiny of where each could stand by decade’s end. A five-year modeling exercise pegging both stocks from their current levels suggests that a $10,000 position in Nvidia reaches approximately $21,170 in the base case, against roughly $19,438 for the equivalent Palantir stake. The upside scenarios are closer than that gap implies: Nvidia’s bull case produces $24,157, while Palantir’s bull outcome reaches $22,925, a difference of just over $1,200. The real divergence emerges at the bottom, where Nvidia’s bear case still returns $14,869 against Palantir’s $12,770, a shortfall of $2,099 that reflects the software company’s more stretched starting valuation. Nvidia’s financial momentum is substantial, with fiscal Q2 2027 revenue hitting $96.22 billion, a 105.8% year-over-year gain, driven by Data Center sales of $89.02 billion alone. The company guided third-quarter revenue to $108 billion, and its Vera Rubin platform, which began shipping in August, is expected to represent the fastest product ramp in Nvidia’s history. Palantir’s own numbers are striking: third-quarter revenue climbed 95.9% to $2.31 billion, and U.S. commercial revenue of $984 million exceeded government contract revenue for the first time. Management raised full-year guidance to between $8.530 billion and $8.534 billion, and the company posted a Rule of 40 score of 158%, far above the 40-point threshold considered a marker of healthy software growth. Palantir CEO Alex Karp echoed his counterpart’s confidence, telling analysts “We really cannot satiate demand.” Yet Palantir’s contract fundamentals present a complication: total contract value expanded just 6% even as reported revenue surged 96%, a disconnect that raises questions about the durability of near-term growth rates. Stock-based compensation at Palantir climbed to $318.9 million from $172.3 million, and receivables rose to $1.88 billion, adding further pressure to an already demanding valuation profile. Nvidia carries its own risks, including gross margins expected to compress to the 71%-72% range as memory costs increase, a near-total absence of China data center revenue in its forward outlook, and roughly $50 billion committed to advanced AI lab investments. With a beta of 2.247, Nvidia’s shares tend to move far more violently than the broader market in either direction, a characteristic that amplifies both the opportunity and the danger. Wall Street’s consensus price target for Nvidia sits at $327.14, supported by 49 Buy ratings and 10 Strong Buy ratings, compared to Palantir’s consensus of $217.97 across a more divided analyst community that includes Hold and Sell ratings. For investors weighing these two AI plays, the numbers suggest Nvidia holds a modest edge across all modeled scenarios, while Palantir’s wider outcome range means both greater potential pain and, in a favorable environment, a result not far behind. For the first time in 33 years, Nvidia is being run by someone other than Jensen Huang, and some of the loudest voices in the market are already lining up behind the person filling his seat. Jim Cramer, Ross Gerber, Daniel Newman, and Kevin O'Leary have all voiced support for interim CEO Colette Kress as the chipmaker enters a new chapter. That backing arrives at a shaky moment. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% at the open and were down about 5% by the time trading settled on Nov. 12, the day the company confirmed Huang's departure. The big question now is whether Kress can steady the world's most closely watched AI company until the board settles on a permanent leader. Cramer had already warned investors to prepare for a future without Huang, but once the resignation landed, his view shifted to backing the person now in the seat. Cramer did not hold back. Speaking on CNBC, he described Kress as a tough, "no-nonsense" executive who "runs with a steel fist." He added that "she is absolutely the one you need right now" because she commands authority and has no patience for nonsense. His view is shaped by years of dealing with her directly. Cramer noted that Kress has led Nvidia's earnings conference calls and has been his main contact at the company, alongside Huang, for a long time. Also read: Michael Burry has a surprising new take on Nvidia stock Kress brings a long record to the job. She has been Nvidia's chief financial officer since September 2013 and held senior finance roles at Texas Instruments, Microsoft, and Cisco before that. She also holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. During her time as CFO, Nvidia's yearly revenue grew from about $4 billion to more than $200 billion, as reported by Al Jazeera. Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management, said he was "very pleased" with the promotion and called Kress "more than prepared and capable to help lead Nvidia." He also argued the company has "a deep bench of highly skilled leaders," adding, "It's their time to step up." Newman, who runs Futurum Group, said Kress "has always impressed me in our conversations." He expects Nvidia's long-term leadership to be "much more of an operations-centric leadership team" focused on "maniacal execution," similar to what Tim Cook was to Steve Jobs at Apple. "There is no replacing Jensen," he wrote on X. That bench is about to be tested like never before. Huang ran a flat organization with about 60 direct reports, and he left behind no heir apparent or succession plan. He also owns only about 3.5% of the company and has no supervoting rights, TechCrunch reported. Some analysts see Kress' long tenure as a real advantage. KeyBanc's John Vinh called her appointment constructive, "given her tenure as CFO since 2013 and deep institutional knowledge of Nvidia's business and strategy." O'Leary went a step further and made the case for Kress to keep the job. He said she "knows the business, the deals, the production schedule, and how the chips get to customers." O'Leary also suggested giving her a few quarters to show what she can do, arguing that Nvidia should consider promoting from within. Not everyone shares that optimism. Michael Burry summed up the moment with "The Don has fallen" and argued that neither Kress nor an outside hire could step into Huang's role without disruption. He also claimed that Nvidia pushed customers to buy chips before their data centers were ready, while stressing that he was not alleging fraud, as reported by TheStreet. He said he isn't worried about near-term damage to the business but questioned "the ability of any new CEO to truly fill Jensen's shoes," according to Yahoo Finance. Part of the worry is how much of the AI ecosystem leaned on Huang personally. In January, Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave, which rents out Nvidia chips to customers such as Microsoft and OpenAI. Nvidia said on Nov. 12 that Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately. Kress will lead the company while keeping her finance duties, and the board will consider both internal and external candidates for the permanent role. "The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team," Chair Harvey Jones said, according to Nvidia. The exit capped a turbulent week. It followed disclosures of extramarital relationships and questions about a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, though the espionage claims have not been established and China has denied them. Three House committee chairs also asked Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18. Kress will not have long to settle in. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Nov. 17, which will offer the first public look at the company without Huang in charge. For Cramer, Gerber, Newman, and O'Leary, that call will be the first chance to see whether their faith in her steel fist holds up. Elon Musk wants Jensen Huang back in charge of Nvidia [NASDAQ: NVDA] — and he's putting his name on it. "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I'm signing it too," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO [NASDAQ: TSLA] posted on X on Nov. 13. He isn't alone. As of 10:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 14, an online letter called Stand with Jensen listed more than 100,000 names — including more than 5,000 people who say they currently work at Nvidia. Huang co-founded the chipmaker in 1993 and led it for 33 years, building it into one of the world's most valuable companies. Nvidia announced Nov. 12 that he had resigned as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately. The board accepted his resignation Nov. 11, according to a regulatory filing. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and director Harvey Jones became the board's first-ever chair. His exit came after reports that he'd had extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect was recruited by China's top spy agency. Huang has admitted to an affair. Neither he nor Nvidia has been charged with any wrongdoing thus far. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change The Stand with Jensen letter asks the board to "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interests." Beyond reinstatement, the letter asks the board to disclose the scope, independence and timeline of its investigation, give Huang a chance to respond before any final decision, and publicly explain the evidence behind his removal. The signers say they haven't been shown evidence that the woman at the center of the controversy was a spy, and argue Huang deserves "due process, not mob justice." The site says it isn't affiliated with Nvidia or Huang. Signers identify themselves, and organizers say they may hold new signatures for review before counting them. At this point, the site's live tracker broke the names down like this: Numbers are moving fast, and this is probably already out of date. For context, Nvidia had about 42,000 employees at the end of its last fiscal year in January, according to its annual report, so the self-identified current staff would represent roughly 12% of the company. Musk is listed at the top as a shareholder, alongside Replit CEO Amjad Masad; Gavin Baker, managing partner of Atreides Management; Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney; and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Cohere's Aidan Gomez and Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani are listed as partners. Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke replied "You have my sword" to Musk's petition post, though Moneywise didn't find his name on the list. Identities on the site are self-reported, and the list includes entries that appear to be fake or duplicated, including at least one offensive name listed as a current Nvidia employee. There's even an unverifiable entry for actress Sydney Sweeney listed as a shareholder. The totals are best read as a rough gauge of support rather than a true headcount. The pushback started inside the company. A longtime engineer posted to Nvidia's internal suggestion box urging the board to weigh employee sentiment before acting, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired. The post has drawn more than 1,600 comments, several asking the board to find a way to bring Huang back. One employee sent a companywide email demanding transparency about Huang's exit, writing: "I stand by Jensen." About two dozen employees posted support on LinkedIn, and Moneywise couldn't find any employee posts backing his departure. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," one employee told Wired. In an informal poll, we asked Moneywise followers whether Nvidia should bring Jensen back. Of 164 votes, 82% said "most definitely." Just 6% said "absolutely not," while 12% picked "he's poaching them all," a nod to the idea that Nvidia employees would follow Huang wherever he goes next. The post follows days of public support from Musk. On the night of Nov. 11, before Huang resigned, Musk replied "That would be an honor" to a ZeroHedge post urging him to hire Huang. The next day, he answered "True words" to AngelList co-founder Naval Ravikant, who wrote that "one does not just simply replace the founder," pointing to Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick. When Ravikant followed up by calling Huang "the Steve Jobs of Nvidia" and "irreplaceable," Musk replied "True." He also replied "Always" to a post praising him for being a true friend to Huang. The two go back years. In May, Musk replied "True" to a repost of photos of the pair taken a decade apart, captioned "The most important thing in life is having true friends." Musk also has a business stake in the outcome. His rocket and AI company, SpaceX [NASDAQ: SPCX], has committed to building its AI data centers exclusively with Nvidia chips, and Nvidia owns a stake in SpaceX worth billions. The petition site also lists him as an Nvidia shareholder. Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors Since resigning, Huang has kept a low profile. Photos published by the Daily Mail show friends and family gathering at what the outlet described as his $38 million Pacific Heights mansion in San Francisco in the hours after he stepped down, as food deliveries, including bags of fried chicken, arrived at the door. Washington isn't done with him. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang agreed to come in. Three House committee chairs then asked him to sit for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1, giving him until 8 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 to confirm or face a subpoena. It wasn't immediately clear whether Huang had confirmed in writing by the deadline. Senate Banking Committee chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., has separately asked Huang to testify on Dec. 3. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whom Scott also called to testify, has agreed to appear. The petition's backers argue the board moved before the facts were in, and the central question is still open. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Nov. 12 there had been "no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice, or by me" about whether Alice Huang was a spy, according to Reuters. title: Think Nvidia Stock Is a Bargain? 6 Reasons the Face of the AI Build-Out Can Plunge Another 50% Following Jensen Huang's Resignation. - The Motley Fool
content:
Although Nvidia stock hasn’t been this fundamentally cheap in a long time, a mountain of risks far outweigh the reward. For the better part of the last four years, no trend has captured the attention and capital of investors quite like the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). Empowering software and systems with the tools to make split-second, autonomous decisions is a $22.5 trillion global addressable opportunity through 2031, according to IDC. Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) is at the center of this addressable market. Nvidia's several generations of graphics processing units (GPUs) are what make AI-accelerated data centers tick, and its CUDA software platform is central to maximizing the potential of these GPUs and keeping clients loyal to its brand. In other words, there were tangible reasons behind Nvidia's ascent to a greater-than-$5 trillion market cap. But as of the closing bell on Nov. 12, Nvidia stock has plummeted 32% from its all-time intra-day high of $243.37, set on Oct. 6. The latest downside catalyst is the resignation of co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang. Jensen Huang's resignation creates a host of problems for the trillion-dollar company he built. Image source: Nvidia. While Nvidia stock hasn't been this fundamentally cheap in a long time, there are half a dozen reasons to believe that the face of the AI infrastructure build-out can plunge another 50%. On Nov. 12, Huang resigned following the admission of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as reports of a separate extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. Unfortunately, his resignation doesn't end the controversy or questions at the company he built from the ground up. For starters, external investigations will continue, despite Huang's resignation. This includes congressional investigations into national security issues, potentially including Nvidia's dealings with China. In short, Huang's departure doesn't put an end to any legal ramifications Nvidia might face. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,116,882 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, CEO Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, President, and member of the Board of Directors, effective immediately. https://t.co/IJE8wWvcrR Huang's departure also strips Nvidia of its identity. He was arguably the face of the AI revolution and was instrumental in orchestrating countless large-scale investments, which some Wall Street analysts have described as "circular." Without Huang at the helm, collaborations may slow. Lastly, Huang's resignation is a blow to investors' and businesses' trust in Nvidia. As Warren Buffett once opined, "It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it." Midterm elections also dealt Nvidia and the AI infrastructure build-out a surprise blow. On the one hand, prediction markets correctly forecast that Democrats would sweep Congress. What wasn't expected was the gubernatorial blue wave. Democratic candidates flipped five gubernatorial seats held by Republicans, including in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. President Donald Trump favors as little AI regulation as possible and has cautioned that he'll "veto everything" that comes to his desk from a Democrat-led Congress. Meanwhile, most Democratic lawmakers prefer to limit data center expansion and beef up the vetting/testing of large language models. While Trump's veto works on Capitol Hill, it'll offer no solace in core data center build-out states, such as Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, where Democratic governors could slow or halt new approvals. That's bad news for all AI hardware stocks, including Nvidia. We're also seeing evidence that the Federal Reserve may get more aggressive with its fourth rate-hiking cycle of the 21st century. In addition to the normal inflationary factors observed in an expanding economy, President Trump's tariffs, the Iran war, and even the AI infrastructure build-out are contributing to persistently elevated inflation. The AI boom is transforming one of the biggest deflationary forces into a key source of US inflation:

Import prices for computer and electronic products surged +7.4% in the first 6 months of 2026, to 77.1 points, the highest since January 2016.

This also marks a +8.0% YoY jump, the largest annual increase on record.

This represents a historic reversal from a downtrend which persisted for over two decades.

Between 2006 and 2019, computer and electronic product import prices fell -30%, as improving technology and manufacturing efficiency consistently pushed costs lower.

Now, the AI investment boom is straining manufacturing capacity for semiconductors, servers, and electronic components, as companies race to build out AI infrastructure regardless of cost.

The AI revolution has flipped technology from a long-term source of deflation into a major driver of inflation. Insatiable demand for Nvidia's GPUs, coupled with ongoing supply shortages, has afforded the company never-before-seen pricing power. Unfortunately, this margin-fueling pricing power has worked its way down the line to everyday consumers. Higher costs for central processing units, hard disk drives, memory, and so on have lifted the prevailing inflation rate. If the Federal Reserve starts aggressively raising interest rates, making borrowing costlier, it would likely clobber the prominently debt-financed AI data center build-out. The bond market gives AI investors reason for pause, as well. While some hyperscalers and neoclouds are financing their AI data center expansions with cash on hand, many are turning to corporate debt issuances. When public companies issue debt, it's typically priced at a par value of $1,000, which financial websites commonly express as $1. When a corporate bond trades at or near its par value, it indicates that traders expect a company to meet its debt obligations. Credit markets are flashing WARNING SIGNS across the AI trade:

Oracle, $ORCL, 5-year credit default swap (CDS) spread has surged to ~263 basis points, while SpaceX's has risen to ~203 basis points, both at record highs.

At the same time, CoreWeave's $CRWV, 5-year CDS is up to a record 982 basis points.

This comes as tech companies have issued nearly $500 billion in new debt this year to finance AI infrastructure, with 9 US investment-grade bond deals worth at least $25 billion each.

The growing debt burden is colliding with uncertainty over whether AI revenues will justify the enormous spending.

As a result, investors are increasingly demanding higher compensation to take on credit risk.

Oracle's market-implied 5-year default risk has risen above 20%, compared with around 16% for SpaceX and more than 7% for Nvidia.

The pressure could intensify further, with Goldman Sachs projecting hyperscaler debt issuance to jump from $250 billion in 2026 to a massive $420 billion in 2027, as 35% of next year's capital spending is expected to be debt-funded.

The AI boom is now testing credit markets, as investors begin repricing the risks behind Big Tech's unprecedented borrowing spree. However, bond prices for several prominent hyperscalers and neoclouds have been plunging throughout 2026, sending bond yields notably higher. The 2056 notes issued in June by Elon Musk's Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -0.59%) recently hit an all-time low of $0.83, while Nvidia's 2060 notes reached a record low of less than $0.62 on Nov. 12. The bond market is sending an unmistakable warning that the AI build-out and/or the companies behind it aren't sustainable. History can also serve as an excellent teaching tool for those investors willing to listen. Dating back to the advent and proliferation of the internet in the mid-1990s, every next-big-thing innovation has navigated an early-innings bubble-bursting event. This includes the internet, genome decoding, nanotechnology, 3D printing, blockchain technology, and the metaverse. The reason these bubbles form is that retail investors consistently overestimate how quickly new technologies will be adopted and/or optimized. AI doesn't have an adoption problem. Nvidia's triple-digit data center sales growth in its fiscal second quarter (ending July 26) confirms that businesses have welcomed this technology with open arms, just as they did with the internet. But businesses weren't able to optimize internet-driven solutions until well after the dot-com bubble had burst. All game-changing technologies need ample time to mature, and it'll likely be years before businesses begin maximizing the returns of their hefty AI investments. This leaves the stock market, and Nvidia, exposed to a possible bubble-bursting event. Last but certainly not least, history tells us that ultra-premium stock valuations aren't sustainable. While Nvidia's valuation has, as noted, come way down, the S&P 500's (^GSPC -0.40%) Shiller Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio (CAPE Ratio), reached its second-highest multiple in 156 years in early June. The AI data center build-out, led by Nvidia, is a big reason for this parabolic increase in stock valuations. Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt History shows that CAPE Ratios above 30 have historically, without fail, foreshadowed declines of 20% to 89% in Wall Street's major stock indexes. Consider it one of Wall Street's virtually surefire red flags. If history rhymes yet again, the companies that led the S&P 500 higher, such as Nvidia, would likely be among the hardest hit. Though some investors see this 32% drawdown as a buying opportunity in the wake of Jensen Huang's resignation, I view it as the start of a much steeper decline in Nvidia stock. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares fell to roughly $165 this week, after the company announced that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president and CEO, effective immediately. He also left the board. CFO Colette Kress will serve as the interim CEO of the tech giant, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. The search will include both internal and external candidates. The SEC filing announcing Huang's resignation doesn't give a reason, but the board was reportedly considering ousting Huang over several recently revealed personal conduct issues, including reports of an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, allegations China has denied. I won't rehash the recent news too much, but wanted to focus on one question that is likely on many investors' minds. After the recent drop, Nvidia trades about 33% below its all-time high, set less than six weeks ago. Is this a buying opportunity? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Nvidia's board says it expects operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap to continue without interruption. And to put it mildly, Nvidia's business is in great shape. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenue rose 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, and data center revenue jumped 117%. Management guided for about $108 billion in third-quarter revenue. Speaking of third-quarter revenue, Nvidia is set to report its latest results on Tuesday (Nov. 17) after the market's close, and its leadership will hold its conference call at 5 p.m. ET. So, we'll have updated numbers in the very near future. Of course, Huang wasn't just any CEO. He co-founded Nvidia and led it for more than three decades, and its early bet on AI computing was largely his vision. He was the face of Nvidia's success and arguably the public face of the entire AI boom. Nvidia's board moved quickly to fill the gap. CFO Colette Kress is now serving as interim CEO and will keep her CFO duties until the board names a permanent leader. Kress has led Nvidia's finance organization since 2013, and before that she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies such as Cisco (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). The board also named Harvey Jones, the former CEO and executive chairman of chip-design software company Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS), as its first-ever chair. That's a big change for a company so closely tied to its founder, and appointing a chair from outside management could give the board more oversight as it looks for Huang's replacement. As mentioned in the last section, the first major test comes on Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports third-quarter results. I'll be listening closely for any change in tone about demand, the product roadmap, and the CEO search. Here's the million-dollar question, and it's a difficult one to answer. On the surface, Nvidia's stock looks remarkably cheap. At a share price of about $163, Nvidia trades at roughly 11 times forward earnings, and this is for a wildly profitable company that just doubled its revenue. Nvidia also has a $235 billion buyback authorization in place, and the new lower share price makes each dollar it spends on repurchases go further. On the other hand, it's fair for the market to put a discount on a company that just lost its founder without warning. Plus, the market has obviously been pricing in an eventual deceleration in revenue growth. In simple terms, at some point the numbers become too large for 100% year-over-year growth to be sustainable. And even after falling more than 30%, Nvidia is still worth nearly $4 trillion. In short, there are solid cases to be made for and against buying the stock right now. Nvidia is on my watch list, and the recent plunge in the stock has my attention. But I'm in no rush to buy. I want to hear what management says on Nov. 17 and see how the CEO search starts to take shape before I make a decision. The bottom line is that if the business keeps executing as it has, today's price could look like a bargain in hindsight, but I'm happy to wait a few days for the dust to settle. It was also alleged the woman, named Alice Huang (no relation), was helping smuggle advanced AI chips to China. On Nov. 11, the New York Times reported Huang also allegedly had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare. Nvidia's code of conduct tells employees to avoid any situations that can create conflict, including "personal relationships." Huang officially resigned as Nvidia's CEO the following morning. That same day, Reuters reported the former CEO had an "intimate relationship" with a second Nvidia employee, though she remains unnamed. Investors are questioning what the future of Nvidia — and the AI boom — will look like without Huang, who co-founded the chipmaker in 1993. The scandal has already had a stunning impact on the company. Nvidia shares plummeted 14% after the market opened following Huang's resignation, wiping out roughly $546 billion in market value. The stock did rebound during the day and was down 4.3% when the market closed. As of Nov. 13, the stock was trading at around $160, down 6.3%. Lawmakers could also target the Trump administration, which has faced allegations that it ignored sales of Nvidia's chips to China, which is currently banned. If you hold NVIDIA inside a traditional IRA, that drop changes the math on a Roth conversion. Treasury rules treat the converted balance as gross income “for the taxable year in which the amount is distributed or transferred from the traditional IRA” (26 CFR 1.408A-4, A-7). Inside an IRA, what you originally paid for the shares doesn’t matter. The fair market value on the day the shares move is taxed as ordinary income. Capital gains rates don’t apply. So the tax bill stays the same while the share count changes. At $166.19, $300,000 moves about 1,726 shares. At the Oct. 6 close — NVIDIA’s highest since June — the same dollar amount would have moved about 1,254 shares, or roughly 472 fewer. If the stock rebounds, that gain builds up inside the Roth tax-free. If it keeps falling, the couple has paid tax on value that is gone, and a conversion can no longer be reversed by recharacterization (26 U.S.C. § 408A(d)(6)(B)(iii)). Consider a married couple, both turning 67 in 2026, filing jointly, with $2.4 million in savings, mostly in a pre-tax IRA holding NVIDIA. They have $100,000 of other fully taxable income, haven’t yet claimed Social Security, have no nondeductible IRA basis, and convert $300,000 of shares in kind. 1. Income with the conversion: $100,000 + $300,000 = $400,000. 2. Subtract the tax year 2026 joint standard deduction of $32,200: taxable income is $367,800. 3. Apply the 2026 joint brackets: 10% on the first $24,800 = $2,480. 12% on $76,000 = $9,120. 22% on $110,600 = $24,332. 24% on $156,400 = $37,536. Total: $73,468. 4. Without the conversion, taxable income is $67,800. Tax is $2,480 + $5,160 = $7,640. 5. Tax caused by the conversion: $73,468 minus $7,640 = $65,828, or 21.9% of the amount converted. The couple still has $35,750 of room before the 32% bracket begins at $403,550 for 2026. The example leaves out the extra standard deduction for taxpayers 65 and older and the new senior deduction, which shrinks as income rises, for simplicity. State income tax would come on top. Paying the $65,828 from a taxable account keeps all of the shares compounding in the Roth. Withholding the tax from the IRA instead means less money lands in the Roth. Under 2026 CMS figures, joint modified adjusted gross income above $342,000 and up to $410,000 raises the Part B premium to $527.50 a month per person, up from the standard $202.90. Part D adds $60.40 a month. If that tier applied to both spouses for a full year, the extra cost would be $9,240. CMS bases these surcharges on income reported on tax returns, and the income is looked back on. That means a 2026 conversion raises premiums in a later year, under that year’s brackets. 1. Year-end deadline: Income is taxed in the year the money leaves a traditional IRA (26 CFR 1.408A-4, A-7), so a 2026 conversion has to be completed by December 31. 2. Five-year clock: A tax-free qualified distribution requires age 59½ plus a five-taxable-year period that starts with the first year of any Roth contribution (§ 408A(d)(2)(B)). 3. RMDs first: Someone turning 67 in 2026 was born in 1959, which sets the RMD age at 73. After that, the year’s required distribution can’t be converted (26 CFR 1.408A-4, A-6). Roth owners face no RMDs while alive. 4. Pro-rata basis: If you have any after-tax IRA basis, Section 408(d)(2) spreads it across all your IRAs, and Form 8606 tracks it. 5. Same single stock: A conversion changes the account type and nothing else. All the Nvidia risk moves into the Roth with the shares. The numbers favor converting if you expect the same or a higher bracket once RMDs begin on a large IRA balance, can pay the tax from outside savings, have a horizon longer than five years, or want to leave tax-free assets to heirs. Converting works poorly if you would have to pay the tax out of the IRA, expect lower income later, plan to leave the account to charity, are close to a Medicare surcharge tier, or might need the money soon. content: HYPE falls toward $69 despite soaring Nvidia futures activity on Hyperliquid. Can the token defend $67 or will a deeper correction follow? Hyperliquid's HYPE token has fallen toward $69 after a roughly 7% pullback from recent trading levels, even as Nvidia-linked perpetual futures attract substantial activity across the decentralized exchange. The divergence has become increasingly noticeable following heightened volatility in Nvidia shares, which encouraged traders to seek round-the-clock exposure through Hyperliquid's HIP-3 derivatives infrastructure. Hyperliquid's Nvidia perpetual futures have become one of the platform's most closely watched markets following the semiconductor company's leadership turmoil. Our earlier Nvidia futures investigation examined reports that the Trade.xyz-operated contract reached $2.14 billion in daily trading volume. That reported peak has not been independently confirmed against archived exchange data. However, the underlying market expansion is established. Hyperliquid's official HIP-3 documentation allows independent operators to launch perpetual futures using its trading infrastructure. The protocol requires market deployers to stake HYPE, creating a direct utility requirement for the token. Hyperliquid has also expanded into traditional financial derivatives, including stock indices and commodity-linked contracts. Nevertheless, increased futures turnover does not automatically produce equivalent spot-market buying demand for HYPE. Under Hyperliquid's official fee structure, trading activity generates fees distributed through the protocol's established mechanisms. Its Assistance Fund automatically converts eligible fees into HYPE, which is subsequently burned, reducing token supply. That mechanism creates a relationship between trading revenue and HYPE demand, but the amount captured depends on fee tiers, market configuration and revenue sharing. The protocol also supports staking discounts, while independent market deployers receive portions of trading fees. Growing derivatives adoption has attracted institutional interest, including Ripple Prime's commodity integration. Separately, Hyperliquid Strategies' $3.5 billion treasury illustrates how some public-market investors have gained substantial exposure to HYPE. However, treasury holdings, derivatives turnover and protocol revenue measure different things and should not be treated as interchangeable indicators of token demand. Kraken's November 14 market data placed HYPE around $69, with a recent trading range extending from approximately $67.22 to $75.11. The $67-$68 region is therefore an immediate downside area to monitor, although it is too early to establish it as a durable support zone. If sellers push HYPE decisively below $67, the psychological $65 level could become the next downside target. A deeper breakdown might bring $60 into consideration, particularly if broader cryptocurrency selling accelerates. Conversely, reclaiming $72 would improve the short-term picture, while a move through $75 could indicate that buyers are regaining control. The company's quarterly reports are normally a marquee event on Wall Street as it's seen as the bellwether for the AI boom. However, this report has particular importance as it will be the company's first without Huang as CEO, and it comes shortly after the crisis that led to his resignation. For investors, the fallout does present potential opportunity. Nvidia stock tumbled last week as the ordeal unfolded, losing 15%, and is now down a third from its peak in October. So is the stock a buy ahead of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday? Let's take a look at what to expect. Nvidia has delivered blowout numbers since the beginning of the AI era, and it's set to do it again on Tuesday. Analysts expect revenue to jump 90.7% to $108.7 billion and for adjusted earnings per share to nearly double from $1.30 to $2.47. Those numbers closely reflect Nvidia's guidance, and the company has a history of edging past its own outlook, so it's a good bet to do so again. Investors also typically pay close attention to Nvidia's performance in the data center segment, its gross margin, and its guidance for the current quarter. However, given the unique circumstances following Huang's departure, those concerns are likely to take a back seat to how CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress handles the earnings call and any discussion about strategy going forward. Typically, Huang and Kress were the only ones on the call, so who else she includes could offer a hint at the company's next CEO or just at who's being elevated in the current regime. The company is likely to avoid questions about the CEO transition or any legal consequences it may face for possible chip export violations. We may get a blanket statement or update from the company at the top of the call, but Kress and her team will likely focus on the usual business. Following its pullback since the peak in October, Nvidia is about as cheap as it's ever been trading at a forward P/E of just 11. Given its growth rate around 90%, that makes the stock look like a stunning bargain. However, the circumstances have changed for the company since Huang's departure, and it now faces a massive risk that it didn't before. Replacing Huang without losing any of the value he brought to the company will be very difficult, and there isn't another person who would readily match his credibility and relationships with employees, customers, suppliers, and governments, his strategic vision for the company and AI, and his intimate knowledge of Nvidia and its product roadmap. Of course, Huang's reputation is tarnished now, but still, some hedge fund managers have called for him to be reinstated, and hundreds of employees signed a letter demanding the same. Nvidia isn't going to overcome this distraction with one earnings call, and I think there is more that can go wrong on Tuesday than can go right. Kress may handle the call adroitly and credibly present herself as a worthy caretaker, but even a good performance doesn't solve the underlying challenges facing Nvidia in Huang's absence. Alternatively, an earnings call that leaves more questions unanswered and makes Huang look irreplaceable could hammer the stock. While Nvidia's valuation may intrigue investors looking to buy the dip, this sell-off is about more than an earnings miss or a short-term business challenge. Management will have to assuage a lot of doubts before Nvidia stock can recover its losses, and that will take time. Given that, investors are better off staying on the sidelines for Tuesday's earnings report. Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned under pressure from the board. The one-two punch of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, and then news of another one with an Nvidia executive (plus a third with an unnamed employee revealed Thursday afternoon) turned out to be too much for the company's board to ignore. That entire web is under the microscope now. What this means for earnings? Not much, beyond all the questions Kress will have to answer. That quarter is over. But all eyes will be on the outlook and on whether Nvidia seems to have its act together. Nvidia stock fell 4.3% the day Huang resigned. title: Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before Nov. 17? - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia stock looks like a bargain, but the value proposition has changed after Huang's exit. All eyes were on Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) this past week as the company's leadership crisis quickly spiraled from a board investigation to the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO. Investor attention is likely to remain on the AI chip leader this coming week, and it's not just because there are so many questions now that Huang is gone. Nvidia will report third-quarter earnings after the bell on Tuesday, Nov. 17. The company's quarterly reports are normally a marquee event on Wall Street as it's seen as the bellwether for the AI boom. However, this report has particular importance as it will be the company's first without Huang as CEO, and it comes shortly after the crisis that led to his resignation. For investors, the fallout does present potential opportunity. Nvidia stock tumbled last week as the ordeal unfolded, losing 15%, and is now down a third from its peak in October. So is the stock a buy ahead of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday? Let's take a look at what to expect. Nvidia has delivered blowout numbers since the beginning of the AI era, and it's set to do it again on Tuesday. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $2,799,718*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Analysts expect revenue to jump 90.7% to $108.7 billion and for adjusted earnings per share to nearly double from $1.30 to $2.47. Those numbers closely reflect Nvidia's guidance, and the company has a history of edging past its own outlook, so it's a good bet to do so again. Investors also typically pay close attention to Nvidia's performance in the data center segment, its gross margin, and its guidance for the current quarter. However, given the unique circumstances following Huang's departure, those concerns are likely to take a back seat to how CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress handles the earnings call and any discussion about strategy going forward. Typically, Huang and Kress were the only ones on the call, so who else she includes could offer a hint at the company's next CEO or just at who's being elevated in the current regime. The company is likely to avoid questions about the CEO transition or any legal consequences it may face for possible chip export violations. We may get a blanket statement or update from the company at the top of the call, but Kress and her team will likely focus on the usual business. Following its pullback since the peak in October, Nvidia is about as cheap as it's ever been trading at a forward P/E of just 11. Given its growth rate around 90%, that makes the stock look like a stunning bargain. However, the circumstances have changed for the company since Huang's departure, and it now faces a massive risk that it didn't before. Replacing Huang without losing any of the value he brought to the company will be very difficult, and there isn't another person who would readily match his credibility and relationships with employees, customers, suppliers, and governments, his strategic vision for the company and AI, and his intimate knowledge of Nvidia and its product roadmap. Of course, Huang's reputation is tarnished now, but still, some hedge fund managers have called for him to be reinstated, and hundreds of employees signed a letter demanding the same. Nvidia isn't going to overcome this distraction with one earnings call, and I think there is more that can go wrong on Tuesday than can go right. Kress may handle the call adroitly and credibly present herself as a worthy caretaker, but even a good performance doesn't solve the underlying challenges facing Nvidia in Huang's absence. Alternatively, an earnings call that leaves more questions unanswered and makes Huang look irreplaceable could hammer the stock. While Nvidia's valuation may intrigue investors looking to buy the dip, this sell-off is about more than an earnings miss or a short-term business challenge. Management will have to assuage a lot of doubts before Nvidia stock can recover its losses, and that will take time. Given that, investors are better off staying on the sidelines for Tuesday's earnings report. title: Is Nvidia Worth This Much Less Without Jensen Huang? - The Motley Fool
content: Last Sunday, Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) co-founder and then-CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with someone who is an alleged Chinese spy. In the following days, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with a direct report. On Thursday, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation. At its peak, Nvidia had a market cap of $5.8 trillion. At market close on Friday, the stock had a market cap of $3.93 trillion. The stock is down 13% over the past week and 6% since Wednesday’s market close. So, investors think Nvidia is worth less without Huang in the corner office. Are they right? There's no doubting the impact that Jensen Huang had on Nvidia's technical abilities. He steered the company to develop cutting-edge products in the GPU realm, along with other products to support them. Nvidia's technology is best-in-class, and with Huang stepping down from the CEO role, that fact likely won't change. Furthermore, while Huang is unique, there are likely a handful of people within the Nvidia organization that could take over and do a great job. The best company at leadership transitions has been Apple (AAPL +0.39%), as it has gone through several transitions and sustained its dominance every time. While Nvidia's situation may be a bit more tumultuous than anything Apple has dealt with, Nvidia can survive. So, investors need to make a decision about Nvidia stock. Is the only reason you invested in it because of Jensen Huang? Or is it because of Nvidia's leading technology and position within the massive AI build-out? For me, I invested in Nvidia because of its products and positioning, although having Huang at the helm was a nice touch. The core of my Nvidia investment thesis is still intact, and even though my position is dipping due to the news breaking this week and investors panic-selling, I'm still holding course because the business will likely be just fine. During last quarter's conference call, Nvidia gave guidance for 70% revenue growth in 2027. Normally, companies don't issue guidance six months in advance, but it's likely that Nvidia has pretty much all of the orders it expects to receive locked in for 2027. It's extremely unlikely that companies will start to cancel orders because of Huang's actions or resignation, so investors should be able to count on that projection. Furthermore, the product development pipeline is already set for many years in advance. So, what's coming out is already influenced by Huang's fantastic technical mind. Even though losing Jensen Huang will hurt Nvidia, I think the business is still a great one and in a fantastic position to deliver incredible returns going forward. Just look at how cheap Nvidia's stock has gotten due to the sell-off. Nvidia trades at about 10 times next year's earnings estimates, which is an incredibly cheap price tag for any stock, let alone one of the world's most dominant companies. While it may take a few months for the storm surrounding Huang to subside, the market will eventually get back to valuing Nvidia's business for what it is, and the stock could provide major upside as a result. title: Nvidia Stock Braces For AI Chipmaker's First Report Without Jensen Huang - Investor's Business Daily
content:
BREAKING: Nasdaq Has Best Week In Two Months, But Ends Below Key Level Nvidia (NVDA) will report its fiscal third-quarter earnings late Tuesday following a headline-grabbing scandal that saw co-founder and Chief Executive Jensen Huang resign in disgrace. Nvidia stock has slumped since the allegations first leaked. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's chief financial officer, will lead the earnings call for analysts. Nvidia investors will be curious if Ian Buck will be on the call. Buck, Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing, has emerged as a leading internal candidate to replace Huang. Wall Street analysts assume a beat-and-raise report is in the cards for Nvidia's Q3 and likely will focus on a future without its rockstar co-founder and artificial intelligence champion. Huang resigned as president, CEO and board member on Thursday after the embarrassing disclosure of two extramarital affairs — one with a subordinate and the other with a reputed Chinese spy. The board of directors is conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia, has been named as a possible replacement for Huang, according to the Financial Times. Nvidia stock plummeted to its lowest level since June 2025 after the CEO change before recovering somewhat as many investors surmised a bottom for the AI leader. But on Friday, Nvidia stock fell again. On the stock market today, Nvidia stock retreated 3% to close at 162.85. Analysts polled by FactSet expect Nvidia to earn an adjusted $2.47 a share, up 90% year over year, on sales of $108.7 billion, up 91%, in its fiscal Q3 ended Oct. 25. For Nvidia's fiscal Q4, FactSet estimates point to the company earning an adjusted $2.74 a share, up 69% year over year, on sales of $124.8 billion, up 83%. However, some analysts have speculated that the AI chipmaker might give cautious guidance, given the upheaval in the C-suite. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that CFO Kress clashed with Huang over his aggressive "circular financing" deals. Under those arrangements, Nvidia provides financing for neoclouds and other companies and that money comes back to Nvidia in the form of semiconductor purchases. Wall Street analysts have expressed worries about Nvidia's financial exposure in the AI data center boom. "This expansion into neoclouds/data centers has forced Nvidia to pivot from a pure chipmaker into an industry financier, exposing its balance sheet to significant credit and real estate risks," Daniel Morgan, senior portfolio manager at Synovus Trust, said in a report. Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, concurred. "The biggest potential risk that we have to look at here is the hundreds of billions of dollars of financing deals that use chips as collateral is at stake," Malek said in a report. "Nvidia is at the center of a very complex web of financing." And the next Nvidia CEO might be more risk-averse, Malek said. Nvidia's problems aren't over after Huang's replacement. The U.S. government is investigating whether his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, facilitated the diversion of Nvidia AI chips into China. And the U.S. will want to know if Kress and other executives were aware of illegal shipments of graphics processing units to China. Meanwhile, Wall Street analysts continue to bail on Nvidia stock. HSBC and GF Securities on Friday downgraded Nvidia stock to hold from buy. Further, Barclays and Rosenblatt Securities added to the long list of investment firms that have cut their price targets on Nvidia stock this week. Nvidia's CEO change is a near-term overhang on its stock, analysts say. But the company's product road map is well established for the next couple of years. "Nvidia's product road map is likely firmly set through at least 2028-2029 and (we) do not believe a new CEO can/will change the road map over the next 2-3 years," Needham analyst Quinn Bolton said in a report Thursday. He rates Nvidia stock as buy with a price target of 200. Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold said the market's reaction to Huang's departure suggests that Nvidia is a "one-man band." "While Jensen Huang has been a standout CEO closely associated with the company, we argue that Nvidia is more than just its CEO," Leopold said in a report Thursday. The second version came on Wednesday, and it handed Ackman his real problem from a direction he hadn't been watching. The New York Times reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reported directly to him. An affair with a direct report breaks the sort of rule a board can enforce without waiting for the FBI to finish its work, and on Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and as a director, effective immediately. Then, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee. If you're keeping score, that makes three reported affairs, and now, zero permanent CEOs. According to CNBC, the board worked late into Wednesday night and made its decision official the next morning. It named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and gave director Harvey Jones the first board chair title in Nvidia's history, and the search for a permanent CEO will consider candidates from inside and outside the company. None of that housekeeping impressed the market. Nividia's stock opened Thursday at $151 and slid to a 52-week low of $148.80 before buyers stepped in, and it closed at $166.19, down 4.34% on the day. Some 735 million shares changed hands, which is 3.75 times the average volume, and the stock is now 31.71% below the $243.37 high it hit on Oct. 6. Wall Street didn't wait around either. Ten analysts downgraded NVDA stock, and Bernstein cut its price target in half to $200. Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon summed up the mood when he said, "We've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines." When Steve Jobs stepped down at Apple (AAPL), Tim Cook had already spent years as the company's chief operating officer. Nvidia's stand-in is its CFO, who now has two jobs while the board looks for someone to take one of them off her plate. Kress has run Nvidia's finances since 2013, and DA Davidson called her "up for the task." Unconventional AI CEO Naveen Rao said the board has three to four months to find a permanent replacement. The bigger issue is that Huang built Nvidia to run through him. He kept 60 direct reports and never named a chief operating officer, which left the company without an obvious second-in-command. So when Newsweek asked governance experts who could replace him, the names beyond Kress included former Google (GOOG) (GOOGL) CEO Eric Schmidt and, of all people, Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook. Baird said on Wednesday that it thinks the odds favor an outside hire over an internal promotion. Wall Street is already putting a price on the uncertainty. Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives cut his fair value estimate for NVDA stock from $300 to $225 after the resignation and called Huang "irreplaceable." Huang's exit also leaves the investigations wide open. He agreed to testify before the House Foreign Affairs Committee before Thanksgiving, and Chairman Brian Mast said Huang "has some very serious questions to answer." Separately, the Justice and Commerce departments are investigating whether a Singaporean company bought advanced Nvidia chips to send to China. Truist, which downgraded the stock to "Hold," said the risks now spread to Nvidia's culture and to whether its chips reached buyers in China. Underneath all the noise, the business numbers are challenging to argue with. Nvidia guided for $108 billion in revenue for the quarter it reports on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and the stock trades at 18 times forward earnings, which is below the sector median of 19.8. Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein called NVDA stock "silly cheap," and even Ives's downsized fair value of $225 is 35% above Thursday's close. This is a hypergrowth business at less than 20x forward earnings now. I'd buy the dip despite all the noise. Nvidia will likely find a solid CEO, and the financials obviously remain rock-solid. title: Breakfast News: What NVDA’s CEO Exit Means for You - The Motley Fool
content: Huang built a company with the products, people, and customers to outlast him, and we expect Nvidia to come through this. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's (NVDA -2.01%) chief executive amid controversies over his personal conduct and questions about whether Nvidia's chips reached China through a customer in Singapore. His exit followed a week of reports about his personal life. The first concerned an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's customers in Singapore. U.S. officials suspected the executive of spying for China, which China denied. On Wednesday, a second relationship, with one of Huang's direct reports, came to light. The board met that night, and the company announced Huang's resignation the following morning. We think investors are right to take Huang's departure seriously. In our view, though, the sell-off prices in more damage than the business has shown so far. If you've followed Nvidia for any length of time, you know how central Huang has been. He co-founded the company in 1993 and led it for all 33 years. His leadership structure was also known for being unusually flat, as he had 33 direct reports at last count, according to CNBC. Huang pushed Nvidia as an innovator and technologist. He launched CUDA (software that lets developers program Nvidia's chips) in 2006 and boldly committed the company to artificial intelligence (AI) computing long before it became a mainstream market. He also managed Nvidia's largest customer relationships himself and represented the company in Washington on export rules for China. That is a lot for one person to hand off, let alone overnight, and Nvidia has no named successor to take it on. For now, CFO Colette Kress, who has worked alongside Huang since 2013 and has joined him on every earnings call, will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $2,116,882 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. We understand why the market reacted so sharply. A company that leaned this heavily on one person's judgment now has to make its next big decisions without him, and under federal scrutiny. Analyst Dan Ives estimates Nvidia is worth 25% to 30% less without Huang, and some discount is warranted. With shares dropping to $148.80 in Thursday trading and closing at around $166, the market has already applied much of it. What reassures us is that Huang's exit on its own is unlikely to change Nvidia's revenue much over the next two years. Demand for its chips is still growing quickly. Last quarter, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, and the company guided to $108 billion for the quarter that ended in October. By any measure, that's a business in good health. Chips take years to design, so the products Nvidia will sell through 2027 were planned while Huang was still in charge, and customers have already ordered many of them. Even if regulators cut off sales routed through Singapore, we estimate Nvidia would lose no more than about 5% of its revenue. A broader crackdown would cost more, and the investigations will help decide whether one comes. title: Nvidia closes below $4T market cap for first time since July 2025 in Huang fallout - CNBC
content:
Nvidia stock sank another 2.01% on Friday, closing below $4 trillion in market cap for the first time since July 2025 as investors navigated the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO, will take over as interim CEO, the company announced Thursday. Following the announcement of Huang’s departure, shares of Nvidia declined sharply Thursday morning before recovering to close just 4% lower. The stock declined 12.75% in the trading week, marking its sixth straight weekly decline and its longest such streak since 2012. Huang was under increasing scrutiny after a series of reports that the CEO was in a relationship with a Chinese woman believed to be a spy for Beijing. Huang disclosed that he had an affair on Sunday in a note to employees. The board also announced an investigation into the matter on Sunday. The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had another extramarital romantic relationship, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia. Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of yet another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC’s request for comment. Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company’s success. Nvidia’s stock was already down more than 20% over the last month. Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF, said much of the company’s success has been built around Huang, and his influence extended into the broader industry. Houri told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe” on Friday that the architecture of the AI industry “really depended on the vision” and expertise of Huang. — CNBC’s Caleigh Keating contributed to this report. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation, and Jensen publicly apologized to his family, employees and shareholders. On November 11, The New York Times reported a second alleged relationship, this time with Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reported to Jensen. To be clear, the allegations involving Chinese intelligence remain unproven publicly, and there’s no established finding that Jensen compromised confidential information. Nvidia (NVDA) stock would likely take a sharp initial hit if CEO Jensen Huang stepped down, but I believe the long-term investment case would remain intact. Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, making his leadership central to the chipmaker's identity and success. Its board is now investigating reports that he was the target of a Chinese intelligence effort. Management has never shared a clear succession plan on who would take over if Huang left, but I'm still bullish on NVDA. The probe hasn't touched the enormous demand for these chips so far, and the stock seems to be priced as if the worst case has happened. As investors and spectators would expect, this probe goes straight to the top. On November 8, the board said a committee of independent directors would run the review with outside counsel. It added that it had no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang is cooperating and stays on as CEO for now, a welcome update from those who have been following the company closely and appreciate the significant role that Huang has played in the development of the sector, and of course the company. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believe she was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over two years. Huang then admitted to a personal relationship with her in a note to staff. Beijing has naturally called the spying claims smears. Of course, this story became highly political almost immediately, and most of Washington isn't letting it go. Three House committee chairs want Huang at a closed-door briefing on November 18, one day after earnings. Committee chair Brian Mast is reportedly weighing a subpoena if Huang says no. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries has also backed limits on chip sales to China in the annual defense bill. Thinking about all of this as a potential investor, Nvidia has surprisingly never named a successor or explained how it would pick one. Semafor found that the word "succession" doesn't appear once in Nvidia's latest annual report. Microsoft (MSFT) uses it 25 times and Alphabet (GOOGL) uses it 16 times. Huang also has more than 50 people reporting directly to him, so there's no obvious number two to step up, with the exception of some family members perhaps. To me, that's a very deliberate move. Huang has said on occasion that planning around a small, hand-picked group of heirs is toxic, and he'd rather grow a wider group of leaders across the company. Asked in January 2026 how long he'd stay, his answer was "for as long as I deserve it." It's worked pretty well so far for shareholders. However, it also leaves the board without a ready answer if it suddenly needs one. Some analysts are now putting a number on that gap. Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less if Huang were removed. Bernstein downgraded the stock to Outperform with a $200 price target. The names floated as potential stand-ins, such as CFO Colette Kress and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, come from media speculation, not from anything the board has actually said. These feel like safe hands to me, but the sheer power of leadership Huang has demonstrated would be almost impossible to match. Meanwhile, the business momentum Nvidia carried into the fall remains hard to ignore. Q2 Fiscal 2027 revenue rose 106% year-over-year to $96.2 billion. Data center sales climbed 117% to $89 billion, and gross margins held at 75%. For Q3, management guided to about $108 billion in revenue, give or take 2%. That outlook notably assumes zero data center compute sales to China. CFO Colette Kress has also said she expects 70% revenue growth in FY28. If Nvidia hits its guide on November 17, the conversation should shift back to demand, at least for a while. Wednesday gave a hint of that. Shares jumped about 5% in early trading after AI cloud provider CoreWeave (CRWV) raised its outlook, which is a reminder that Nvidia's biggest customers are still spending. Even so, the stock is still down about 15% in November. Much of the slide started before the probe, with the stock losing roughly 22% to 24% from its early-October peak through the post-midterm chip sell-off. I would tend to think that a fair amount of the leadership risk is already baked in after such a heavy news event. Nvidia trades at about 21x trailing earnings. On a forward basis, some analysts put the stock at 18.65x. The semiconductor industry's median forward P/E is close to 20.31x, so Nvidia trades at a modest discount of roughly 8% to its peers. Against its own history, the gap is much wider. At 18.65x, the stock is valued at less than half its five-year average of 41.38x, even after more than doubling its sales last quarter. So what's the company worth without its charismatic CEO? At 18.65x, the market is assuming forward earnings of about $9.32 per share. Some analysts speculate that Nvidia without Huang might trade at 10x to 12x, which, by my calculations, comes to roughly $93 to $112. Knock 25% to 30% off today's price, as Ives suggests, and you land at roughly $122 to $130, which is a milder downside than the multiple-compression case. If the board clears Huang and the multiple drifts back toward the sector median of 20.31x, the numbers point to around $189. I'd take that trade, as long as earnings estimates hold up. However, not everyone agrees: Baird cut NVDA to Hold with a $200 target on November 11, and Citi (C) trimmed its target to $225. Wall Street is still firmly behind Nvidia, though the support has thinned slightly this week. NVDA has a Strong Buy consensus based on 29 Buys and seven Holds over the past three months. The average NVDA price target of $290.90 implies 67.44% upside from the last price. For 33 years, Nvidia and Huang have been almost synonymous, and this probe makes it understandable for investors to picture one without the other. With no clear successor, I'd expect a pretty sharp drop if he were forced out. However, the business itself still looks strong, and the shares already trade well below their own history and the sector. I see the current price as a fair entry for long-term investors willing to sit through some near-term noise. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

Bitcoin investors have nobody, and that may be the biggest difference between the two assets. But here's the catch: Wall Street has poured billions into Bitcoin ETF products, which were originally designed to operate without a corporate leader. NVDA stock, meanwhile, carries a CEO premium built around Huang's influence over AI. Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in after-hours trading today, after its board considered Huang's future. The move threatened to erase around $600 billion in market value. Chip demand had not suddenly disappeared. Investor confidence in Nvidia's leader had become the driver. Huang is more than Nvidia's chief executive. He is its chief strategist and public evangelist for the AI boom. Reuters reported that more than 60 executives report directly to him, while analysts see no obvious successor who could replace his influence seamlessly. That concentration creates upside when investors trust the leader. Huang can turn a keynote or forecast into a market-moving event. It also creates vulnerability: investors struggle to separate the person from the company. NVDA stock still symbolizes ownership of chips central to AI infrastructure. Yet reports of a possible leadership change were enough to shake the stock and its partners. It's a CEO premium phenomenon, the confidence investors attach to one individual. Apple offers a historical comparison. When Steve Jobs resigned as CEO on August 24, 2011, Apple shares fell 5.9% in after-hours trading. Tim Cook took over, and the company continued to grow. Apple shares have since climbed 1,946% during Cook's tenure. But what's the difference? Apple had succession planning and an operating business. Bitcoin was built around a different proposition. Satoshi Nakamoto disappeared from public view years ago. Bitcoin kept running. There is no CEO to reassure holders, no board to appoint a successor, and no quarterly call where a founder promises a better product cycle. Its issuance schedule and consensus rules do not depend on a personality. But Bitcoin is not immune to sentiment. Its price still responds to adoption, regulation, security, liquidity, and demand. But its sentiment is less dependent on a single executive. Nobody has to decide whether Satoshi is still the right person for the job. The Bitcoin ETF market shows how much Wall Street has changed the ownership story. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have attracted $55.4 billion in cumulative net inflows since launching in January 2024. The funds held about 1.31 million BTC on November 11, equal to 6.5% of Bitcoin's 20.11 million current circulating supply. BlackRock's IBIT alone held about 793,069 BTC on November 9, worth nearly $59.5 billion. It offers traditional portfolios Bitcoin exposure without wallet or private-key management. This is the Bitcoin ETF Paradox. Wall Street does not control Bitcoin's protocol, but its products now shape a huge part of the market's demand narrative. Inflows can strengthen buying pressure. Redemptions can reverse it. Investors increasingly watch BlackRock and Fidelity flows for clues about institutional appetite. A world without ETFs would look different. The $55.4 billion in net inflows would not have entered through these products. Some investors might have bought Bitcoin directly, used futures, or stayed away. The funds' 1.31 million BTC would have had different owners, and the market would have lost a major regulated route for institutional access. Subtracting $55.4 billion from Bitcoin's market value would not reveal its ETF-free price. Market capitalization is set by marginal trades, not by adding every dollar invested. The real counterfactual concerns demand, access, and who is willing to buy when prices fall. That is where Bitcoin's advantage and its new weakness meet. Nvidia's CEO premium can become a liability when confidence in Jensen Huang cracks. Bitcoin has no founder to lose. Bitcoin never needed Satoshi to keep the network alive. Wall Street, however, has taught a new generation of buyers to watch its flows. The protocol remains decentralized. The investment narrative is increasingly institutional.
